findings.cwe_name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
findings.description: The admin changelist for User lists the 'password' column for every user. If the app's custom User model stores plaintext or weakly hashed passwords, anyone with admin view access, or anyone who can see an admin screen, can read all credentials. Admin-site XSS or shoulder-surfing would expose them as well.

proposal.explanation: Removed the 'password' column from the User admin changelist so credential values (hashed or otherwise) are not displayed to every admin viewer. Also excluded the field from the admin edit form so it is not rendered there either.
proposal.review_notes: Verify that the custom User model has a 'password' field (exclude would error on a nonexistent field only if explicitly referenced in a form; check admin loads). If admins need to set passwords, consider subclassing django.contrib.auth.admin.UserAdmin, which provides a safe password-change form. Separately confirm passwords are stored with a strong hash, since the model is not shown and plaintext storage would remain a vulnerability. Excluding the field may prevent creating users via admin with a password; adjust to your workflow.

findings.cwe_name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
findings.description: The INSERT concatenates self.username and an event string containing blabberUsername and a value read from the database (second-order injection) into the SQL without parameterization.
findings.vulnerable_snippet:
sqlQuery = "INSERT INTO users_history (blabber, event) VALUES (\"" + self.username + "\", \"" + event + "\")"
            self.logger.info(sqlQuery)
            self.cursor.execute(sqlQuery)

edits.replacement:
sqlQuery = "DELETE FROM listeners WHERE blabber=%s AND listener=%s;"
        self.logger.info(sqlQuery)
        try :
            self.cursor.execute(sqlQuery, (blabberUsername, self.username))

            sqlQuery = "SELECT blab_name FROM users WHERE username = %s"
            self.logger.info(sqlQuery)
            self.cursor.execute(sqlQuery, (blabberUsername,))
            result = self.cursor.fetchone()

            event = self.username + " is now ignoring " + blabberUsername + " (" + result[0] + ")"
            sqlQuery = "INSERT INTO users_history (blabber, event) VALUES (%s, %s)"
            self.logger.info(sqlQuery)
            self.cursor.execute(sqlQuery, (self.username, event))

proposal.explanation: All three queries (DELETE, SELECT, INSERT) now use placeholders with values passed as a separate parameter tuple to cursor.execute, so the DB driver binds the values instead of Python building the SQL string. The event string, which includes a value read back from the database, is bound as a parameter in the INSERT, which closes the second-order injection.
proposal.review_notes: This assumes a DB-API driver that uses the %s paramstyle (e.g. mysql-connector or PyMySQL, which fits the MySQL-style original). If the driver uses ? or named placeholders, adjust accordingly. The bare except and the logger.error call with extra args are unchanged and were not part of these findings. The code still assumes the SELECT returns a row (result[0]).

findings.description: The username, blabberUsername, and the blab_name read from the database are concatenated into the INSERT statement. This allows SQL injection, including second-order injection through the stored blab_name.
findings.vulnerable_snippet:

            sqlQuery = "INSERT INTO users_history (blabber, event) VALUES (\"" + self.username + "\", \"" + event + "\")"

edits.replacement:
sqlQuery = "INSERT INTO listeners (blabber, listener, status) values (%s, %s, 'Active');"
        self.logger.info(sqlQuery)
        try :
            self.cursor.execute(sqlQuery, (blabberUsername, self.username))

            sqlQuery = "SELECT blab_name FROM users WHERE username = %s"
            self.logger.info(sqlQuery)
            self.cursor.execute(sqlQuery, (blabberUsername,))
            result = self.cursor.fetchone()

            event = self.username + " started listening to " + blabberUsername + " (" + result[0] + ")"
            sqlQuery = "INSERT INTO users_history (blabber, event) VALUES (%s, %s)"
            self.logger.info(sqlQuery)
            self.cursor.execute(sqlQuery, (self.username, event))

proposal.explanation: All three queries now use the DB-API parameter binding of cursor.execute(query, params). User-controlled values (blabberUsername, self.username) and the stored blab_name, which is embedded in the event string, are passed as bound parameters instead of being concatenated or %-formatted into the SQL. This also closes the second-order injection path. The logged query text now contains only placeholders.
proposal.review_notes: I assumed a driver that uses the %s paramstyle (mysql-connector, PyMySQL, psycopg2), which matches the original code's use of %s. If the driver is sqlite3 or another qmark-style driver, change the placeholders to ?. The existing bare except and the logger.error call with an extra argument were left unchanged. result may be None if the user doesn't exist, which the except block still swallows. Test against the actual database.

findings.cwe_name: Missing Password Field Masking
findings.description: The password and cpassword fields are plain CharFields with no PasswordInput widget. They render as visible text inputs, which exposes the typed password to shoulder surfing and can leave it in browser autofill or history.

findings.cwe_name: Missing Password Field Masking
findings.description: The ModelForm exposes the model's 'password' field without overriding its widget, so it renders as a visible text input instead of a masked password field.

edits.replacement:
password = forms.CharField(max_length=100, widget=forms.PasswordInput)
    cpassword = forms.CharField(max_length=100, widget=forms.PasswordInput)

proposal.explanation: Added forms.PasswordInput widgets so password fields render as masked inputs (type=password) in both the ModelForm and the RegisterForm. Field names, validation, and form structure are unchanged.
proposal.review_notes: PasswordInput does not re-render submitted values by default, so on validation errors users must retype passwords (standard behavior). Note that the ModelForm still handles the password field as a plain model field; storage/hashing is handled elsewhere and was not reviewed. Add autocomplete attributes (e.g., 'new-password') if desired. Not tested.

findings.cwe_name: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information
findings.description: The TOTP secret is stored in plaintext in the database, so a database leak lets an attacker generate valid second-factor codes. The password hint is also stored in plaintext.

edits.replacement:
import secrets
from django.contrib.auth.hashers import make_password

# Random, unguessable initial password; the user must set a real one later
    password = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    dateCreated = moment.now().format("YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss")
    lastLogin = None
    return User(userName, make_password(password), None, pyotp.random_base32(), dateCreated, lastLogin, realName, blabName)

proposal.explanation: The initial password is now a random value from secrets instead of the username. The password hint no longer echoes the username and is set to None, which the field allows. Hashing now uses Django's make_password, which is salted PBKDF2 by default, instead of unsalted MD5. The resulting hash is about 88 characters and fits in the 100-character column. The now-unused hashlib import was replaced by the secrets and make_password imports.
proposal.review_notes: Login and password-reset code is not visible here. If it compares MD5 digests, switch it to check_password, or keep a temporary fallback for legacy MD5 hashes. Confirm that the registration flow sets a real password after create() is called, because the initial password is now unknown to everyone. F0012 is not addressed. Encrypting the TOTP secret and password hint at rest needs key management and a field-level encryption library, which is outside a minimal patch to this file. Also check that any existing code reading password_hint handles None.

findings.cwe_name: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
findings.description: The attacker-controlled HTTP Host header is used to build a URL that the server requests with urllib.request.urlopen. An attacker can make the server send requests to arbitrary internal or external hosts (blind SSRF), for example by sending a crafted Host header.
findings.vulnerable_snippet:
host_ip = request.META['HTTP_HOST'].split(':')[0]
            print("da")
            redir = urllib.request.Request('http://' + host_ip + ':' + request.META['SERVER_PORT'] + '/feed')
            urllib.request.urlopen(redir, timeout=5)

proposal.explanation: The view built a URL from the attacker-controlled Host header and fetched it server-side with urllib.request.urlopen, which is a blind SSRF. The request's result was never used. The except branch always ended in redirect('feed'), and a successful fetch fell through to login(request). I removed the outbound request and redirect to the 'feed' view directly for logged-in users. This is the evident intended behavior, and it no longer makes any server-side request.
proposal.review_notes: One behavior difference: before, if the self-request succeeded (no exception), a logged-in user fell through to login(request). That looks like a bug, since the comment says logged-in users go to the feed. Confirm that redirecting them to the feed is the intended behavior. The now-unused 'import urllib' on line 5 is harmless and can be removed. The debug print statements were removed with the block. Also check that the 'feed' URL name exists.

proposal.explanation: Removed disable_ssl_certificate_validation so httplib2 verifies TLS certificates (F0026). findings.cwe_name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
findings.description: The user-controlled POST parameter 'fortunefile' is interpolated into a shell command passed to os.system without sanitization. An attacker can inject shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /`) to execute arbitrary commands, or read arbitrary files.

findings.cwe_name: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command ('Argument Injection')
findings.description: The user-supplied 'host' value is passed as a positional argument to ping with no validation. Although no shell is used, a value beginning with '-' can be interpreted as an option by ping, enabling argument injection.

proposal.explanation: In fortune(), the os.system call with user input is removed. Only the allowed selections ('fortunes' and 'riddles') are handled, and any other value returns an empty string, which also avoids returning None. In ping(), hosts that start with '-' or contain whitespace are rejected. A '--' separator is added so ping treats the host as a positional argument. The rejection raises inside the existing try block, so it takes the existing error path and returns the 'unknown host' output.
proposal.review_notes: The fix removes the arbitrary-file `cat` fallback; if any legitimate feature relied on it, add an explicit allowlist mapping of names to files. Check that the '--' separator works with the target platform's ping implementation. The existing logger.info("Exit Code:", ...) and logger.error("Error", e) calls are incorrectly formatted logging calls and were left unchanged because they are outside the findings. Nothing was run or tested.

# Supplied via environment; if unset, a random per-process key is generated

SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY') or get_random_secret_key()

# SECURITY WARNING: don't run with debug turned on in production!
DEBUG = os.environ.get('DJANGO_DEBUG', '').lower() in ('1', 'true', 'yes')

# Restrict allowed hosts; override with a comma-separated DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS
ALLOWED_HOSTS = [
    h.strip()
    for h in os.environ.get('DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS', 'localhost,127.0.0.1').split(',')

proposal.explanation: The secret key is now read from DJANGO_SECRET_KEY, with a random per-process fallback instead of a committed key. DEBUG defaults to off and is enabled only through DJANGO_DEBUG. ALLOWED_HOSTS defaults to localhost and 127.0.0.1 and can be set through DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS. SecurityMiddleware and CsrfViewMiddleware are re-enabled.
proposal.review_notes: Nothing was run or tested. The old SECRET_KEY is in version control, so treat it as compromised and rotate any deployment that used it. Enabling CSRF will reject POSTs from forms that lack {% csrf_token %}, and from AJAX calls that lack the X-CSRFToken header. Check the templates and JS. With DEBUG off, runserver no longer serves static files, so set DJANGO_DEBUG=1 for local development or serve static files separately. Set DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS for the real deployment hostnames. SecurityMiddleware only adds nosniff and similar headers by default. HSTS and SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT still need to be configured explicitly for HTTPS deployments. The DEBUG-level root logger is unchanged.
